# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Optical Baseline and SAR Backscatter

The Sentinel-2-only models serve as the primary baseline for this thesis. Their performance on the test set confirms the core finding of the preceding project work [@klaver2025]: pixel-based machine learning models using temporal differences in vegetation indices can detect mowing events with high accuracy when cloud-free imagery is available. The preceding study showed that even a single feature (ndii_diff) can achieve reasonable scene-level performance, suggesting that the mowing signal in optical data is concentrated in a small number of spectral change indicators. The refined feature selection in this thesis, using permutation importance analysis to reduce from 20 candidates to three to five features, confirms this concentration while retaining complementary spectral information (GNDVI, SWIR) that stabilises predictions across varying scene conditions. The additional workflow improvements introduced in this thesis, including threshold calibration and post-processing, proved to enhance performance further and are discussed in more detail below.

The GRD backscatter features showed negligible predictive value for mowing detection at this study site. The GRD-only configuration achieved near-random performance, and adding GRD features to the optical baseline did not improve classification accuracy. This outcome is consistent with the findings of De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021], who reported that SAR backscatter alone is a weak predictor of mowing events due to the confounding influence of soil moisture, precipitation, and phenological variation on the returned amplitude signal. While backscatter changes after mowing are physically expected, particularly a decrease in VH due to the loss of canopy volume scattering, these changes are small relative to the environmental noise floor and do not produce a reliable classification signal at the pixel level.

## Coherence Signal and Its Limitations

The integration of interferometric coherence derived from SLC data was motivated by the physical expectation that mowed grassland, presenting a more stable scattering surface, would produce measurably higher coherence than tall, moving vegetation. The seasonal coherence analysis (@tbl-coherence-seasonal) reveals that this expectation is only partially supported at the Zurich Airport study site.

The expected positive signal, where mowed parcels show higher post-event coherence than unmowed parcels, was observed exclusively for VH polarisation during the late growing season (August to October). In this temporal window, the SNR-corrected VH coherence showed a statistically significant positive Cohen's d with a low p-value, and the density distributions (@fig-vh-density) confirm a visible rightward shift for the mowed class. For VV polarisation, Cohen's d remained near zero across all seasons with consistently high p-values, indicating that co-polarised coherence does not meaningfully differentiate mowed from unmowed grassland at this site. During the early and peak growing seasons, both polarisations showed negative or negligible effect sizes, representing a direct inversion of the expected scattering behaviour.

Several factors contribute to this weak and inconsistent signal. First, the airport grasslands are managed under specific operational protocols that differ from the agricultural grasslands studied in the reference literature [@tamm2016; @devroey2021], with potentially different grass species, cutting heights, and mowing frequencies. Second, the Sentinel-1 repeat cycle of 6 or 12 days means that rapid regrowth during the peak season can substantially reduce the coherence contrast between mowed and unmowed areas before the second acquisition of a pair is recorded. This observation aligns with the findings of Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016], who reported that the 12-day temporal baseline proved insufficient during rapid growth phases. Third, the C-band wavelength of 5.6 cm interacts with vegetation at a scale where even short grass stubble may still produce appreciable volume scattering, reducing the expected coherence increase.

The SNR correction following Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016] consistently improved the statistical separability of the classes by pushing Cohen's d values towards the expected positive direction and lowering p-values across most season and polarisation combinations. However, the correction strictly amplified existing signals rather than reversing the fundamental signal weakness.

These pixel-level findings explain why the coherence-only models achieved near-random F1-Scores (0.468 to 0.479) in both training evaluation and operational application. While the seasonal analysis demonstrates that a coherence signal exists at the parcel level in late season, the per-pixel variability is too high for a
pixel-based classifier to exploit reliably. A parcel-level or segment-based approach, where coherence is averaged over predefined spatial units, could potentially yield better class separability. However, such an approach would sacrifice the ability to detect sub-parcel mowing patterns, which is a relevant use case at the airport where mowing frequently affects only portions of larger grassland areas.

Despite these limitations, including coherence features alongside optical features in the Full-fusion RF configuration produced the highest test-set F1-Score within Group B (0.922) and competitive operational results. This indicates that the classifier can extract some complementary information from coherence that is not captured by optical indices alone, even when the standalone coherence signal is weak. The selective integration strategy, informed by permutation importance analysis, proved essential: adding all available features indiscriminately degraded performance for some classifiers, particularly the SVM, which showed sensitivity to irrelevant features in higher-dimensional input spaces.

## Threshold Calibration and Postprocessing

The scene-level threshold calibration emerged as the single most impactful operational improvement in this thesis. The calibrated thresholds for S2-based models ranged from 0.775 to 0.950, far above the default of 0.5, reflecting the severe class imbalance at scene level where typically less than 10% of grassland pixels are mowed at any given time. On scene 46, threshold calibration alone improved the F1-Score from 0.477 to 0.587, primarily by increasing precision from 0.327 to 0.499 while recall decreased moderately from 0.881 to 0.712 (@fig-threshold-calibration).

This finding has important implications for interpreting the postprocessing results. Spatial postprocessing methods such as morphological filtering and superpixel aggregation are designed to remove isolated false positive pixels, the same type of noise that threshold calibration addresses at the decision level. Because the calibrated threshold already eliminates the majority of scattered false detections, the residual noise available for postprocessing to address is limited. This  explains why the best postprocessing configuration achieved only a marginal improvement of +0.009 F1 over the calibrated baseline, and why the effect was inconsistent across scenes (@fig-pp-f1-comparison). In early experiments using models from the preceding study without threshold calibration, postprocessing produced substantially larger improvements, confirming that the two mechanisms target the same error source.

The poor performance of SLIC-based postprocessing (F1 dropping to approximately 0.235) warrants specific attention. At the tested parameter ranges, the majority voting within superpixel segments was too aggressive: mowing events at this site often affect areas that are small relative to the segment size, causing the mowed pixels to be outvoted by the surrounding unmowed majority within a segment. This suggests that SLIC-based postprocessing would require substantially smaller segments to be viable for this application, at the cost of reduced noise suppression.

## Model Stability Across Scenes

A notable observation across the operational evaluation is the lack of a single consistently best-performing model. On scene 12, the S2-only_diff SVM achieved the highest F1-Score, while on scene 73, the S2-only_best RF performed best. The Full-fusion RF ranked third on both scenes but was never the top performer. Similarly, adding coherence or GRD features marginally improved performance on some scenes while worsening it on others.

This instability extends to the feature importance analysis, where individual feature rankings shifted substantially between Group A and Group B. Features such as gndvi_diff, which showed negative permutation importance in Group A, ranked among the most informative predictors in Group B.

Several factors likely contribute to this variability. The limited number of training events (63 for Group A, 24 for Group B) means that the specific composition of each group, including the seasonal distribution of events, cloud cover patterns, and mowing extent, can disproportionately influence both feature importance estimates and model performance. Scene-level evaluation amplifies this effect because each scene represents a single spatial and temporal snapshot with its own weather conditions, mowing patterns, and ground truth quality. Additionally, the ground truth data were initially recorded by hand on paper maps and subsequently digitised, a process in which spatial accuracy can be lost at both stages. Occasional inconsistencies between model predictions and ground truth labels suggest that some mowing events may have been incompletely recorded (label noise), meaning that the reported model performance likely represents a conservative estimate for certain scenes.

The practical implication is that the choice of model configuration for operational deployment should be based on average performance across multiple scenes rather than on any single evaluation. The S2-only configurations offer the most consistent performance with the least data dependency, making them the most robust choice for operational application at this stage.

## Comparison with PW2 Baseline

The enhanced workflow developed in this thesis substantially improves upon the baseline from the preceding project work across both evaluation scenes. On scene 73, the best current model (S2-only_best RF, F1 = 0.749) nearly doubles the F1-Score of the PW2 model (F1 = 0.397). On scene 12, the improvement is smaller but consistent (0.689 vs 0.597). In both cases, the improvement is driven primarily by precision, which reflects the combined effect of three factors: the expanded multi-feature design captures the mowing signal more robustly than a single vegetation index; the improved ground truth cleaning removes ambiguous training samples at parcel boundaries; and the scene-level threshold calibration adapts the decision boundary to the actual class distribution encountered during application.

These improvements address the core limitations identified in the preceding study. The salt-and-pepper noise that characterised the PW2 full-scene predictions is  substantially reduced, and the model produces spatially more coherent predictions that better correspond to the expected shapes of mowing events.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this study.

The model was trained and evaluated exclusively on grasslands at Zurich Airport. Airport grasslands are managed under specific operational protocols and may not be representative of agricultural or ecological grassland management in other regions. The extent to which the model generalises to other sites, grass species, and management regimes remains largely untested.

The ground truth data were recorded by hand and then digitised, a process that can introduce spatial inaccuracies at both stages. The quality and spatial accuracy of these records directly affect both model training and evaluation. Despite substantial efforts to acquire additional ground truth from external institutions, no datasets with the required spatial and temporal resolution were obtained in sufficient quantity, limiting the study to a single primary reference source.

The coherence features were available for only 24 of the 63 training events due to the strict temporal matching requirements of the quadruplet design and incomplete SLC processing. This reduced sample size for Group B configurations limits statistical power and means that the comparison between S2-only and S2+coherence models operates on different subsets of the data with different event compositions.

The coherence rasters were computed at 20 m resolution and resampled to 10 m to match the optical grid. This resampling introduces spatial smoothing and means that the coherence features do not capture sub-20 m spatial variability. The mismatch in native resolution between the optical and SAR features is a structural limitation of combining these two sensor types.

The current coherence feature design uses only absolute coherence values (coh_vv, coh_vh) from the pre-mowing and post-mowing pairs. Computing a coherence temporal difference analogous to the optical feature design would require six SLC acquisitions per event rather than four, further reducing the number of usable training events and was therefore not pursued. Given the weak pixel-level coherence signal observed at this site, it is uncertain whether the additional temporal information would have produced meaningful improvement.

## Conclusion and Outlook

This thesis investigated whether the integration of SAR interferometric coherence and spatial postprocessing methods can improve automated mowing detection from satellite imagery. The findings can be summarised with respect to the research questions posed in @sec-introduction.

Regarding the integration of SAR data (Q1): GRD backscatter provided no useful signal for mowing detection. Interferometric coherence showed a physically meaningful but weak and season-dependent response that could not support stand alone detection. When selectively combined with optical features, coherence contributed marginal improvements on balanced test sets, but this advantage did not consistently translate to operational scene-level application. The goal of reducing dependence on cloud-free optical acquisitions through SAR data was therefore not achieved in a practically meaningful way.

Regarding spatial postprocessing (Q2): morphological filtering and median pre-filtering produced small, inconsistent improvements in classification F1-Score. The limited impact is attributable to the effectiveness of scene-level threshold calibration, which addresses the same false positive noise that postprocessing targets. SLIC superpixel aggregation degraded performance at the tested parameter ranges.

Regarding ground truth acquisition (Q3): extensive efforts to obtain additional reference data from external institutions were unsuccessful, confirming that the availability of spatially precise mowing records remains the primary bottleneck for scaling and validating mowing detection workflows.

Regarding the comparison with the PW2 baseline (Q4): the enhanced workflow substantially improves upon the baseline, nearly doubling the operational F1-Score on one evaluation scene. The improvement is driven by the multi-feature design, improved ground truth cleaning, and scene-level threshold calibration rather than by the addition of SAR data.

For future work, the most impactful direction would be the acquisition of diverse, spatially precise ground truth data across multiple sites and management regimes. This would enable both robust model validation and the investigation of transferability. For coherence specifically, a parcel-level or segment-based classification approach, where coherence is spatially averaged before classification, could yield better results than the pixel-based approach pursued here, though at the cost of losing sub-parcel spatial resolution. Additionally, computing coherence temporal differences from six-acquisition sequences could provide stronger features, if sufficient SLC data availability can be ensured. Finally, evaluating the operational workflow across a broader range of scenes and years would provide the statistical basis needed to identify a reliably optimal model configuration for deployment.
